pairs.rationale: The question asks what advantage belongs to the Jew and circumcision. The later discussion lists Israelite adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship, promises, fathers and the Christ according to flesh. That list supplies a fuller privilege discussion, not a claim that these advantages exempt anyone from the sin charge developed here.

Romans names being entrusted with God’s oracles as the advantage. Stephen describes Moses receiving living oracles to give to his people in the wilderness. The shared received revelation connects the statements, while the recipients, Sinai setting and singular mediator are not identical formulations.

Romans asks whether some people’s unfaithfulness nullifies God’s faithfulness; the letter says that if we are unfaithful He remains faithful. The shared contrast does not erase the adjacent letter’s warning about denying Him or turn either statement into an unqualified verdict on every individual’s outcome.

The quoted justification-in-God’s-words and prevailing-when-judged language corresponds to this psalm’s confession of sin before God. Romans applies it while insisting on God’s truth against human falsehood. The psalm’s personal confession and the letter’s argument remain distinct, with the actual quotation forms retained.

Romans’s every-human-being-a-liar formula has a close counterpart in the psalm’s every-man-a-liar statement. The psalm attributes its statement to the speaker’s bewilderment; Romans contrasts human falsehood with God’s truth. That framing is not silently transferred between the passages.

Both passages frame a question about unrighteousness with God and reject it. Romans3 raises wrath and explicitly marks human terms; Romans9 raises the question amid the Jacob/Esau and mercy discussion. These are presented objections, not assertions that God is unrighteous.

Paul’s rejection appeals to God judging the world. Abraham likewise appeals to the One judging all the earth doing justice, while pleading against sweeping righteous and ungodly away together. The shared justice premise is used in different arguments, without making the Sodom plea a quotation of Paul’s objection.

The question about personal falsehood advancing divine truth parallels the earlier question about human unrighteousness displaying God’s righteousness. The earlier objection is rejected with an appeal to divine judgment. This identifies the argumentative pattern without treating the question as a confession that Paul lied for God’s glory.

Here Paul condemns the slandered proposal to do evil so good may come. Later he asks whether remaining in sin could increase grace and emphatically rejects it. The proposed benefits differ, but both passages refuse turning a claimed divine good into permission to continue wrongdoing.

Romans charges Jews and Greeks alike with being under sin. Galatians describes Scripture confining everything under sin so that the faith-in-Jesus promise is given to believers. The universal sin language corresponds, while the confinement image and stated promise purpose are the letter’s additional formulation.

Romans opens its Scripture chain with no righteous one, not even one. Ecclesiastes says no righteous person on earth does good without sinning. The shared universal righteousness-and-sin claim has different wording; the link does not identify Ecclesiastes as an indisputable verbatim source of the chain’s opening line.

The psalm describes the Lord’s search for anyone understanding or seeking God, followed by everyone turning aside. Romans gives the negative understanding-and-seeking conclusion within its chain. The psalm’s searching question and ensuing answer are preserved rather than presented as exactly the same sentence.

The all-turned-aside, together-useless and no-kindness-not-one lines closely match the beginning of this saved psalm unit. That original unit continues with additional throat-to-no-fear lines as well; they are not excised or divided into manufactured verse IDs.

The opened-tomb throat and tongues practicing deceit clauses correspond to the psalm’s throat and tongue description. The psalm also speaks about mouth and heart, which Romans does not repeat in these clauses. The separate asp-poison clause is not assigned to this target.

The asp poison beneath the lips corresponds to this psalm’s asp venom beneath their lips. The target also compares sharpened tongues with a serpent. The shared lip-and-asp image is precise, while poison/venom rendering and the additional tongue line remain as saved.

Both lines describe a mouth full of cursing and bitterness. The psalm uses his mouth and also includes deceit; Romans uses their mouth and omits that third item here. The quotation correspondence does not erase those pronoun and list differences.

Romans’s feet swift to pour out blood corresponds to Isaiah’s feet running toward wickedness and quick to shed blood. The bloodshed image is shared, while the extra wickedness and foolish-thought clauses are not inserted into Paul’s shorter line.

The ruin-and-misery-in-their-ways line corresponds to Isaiah’s destruction and misery in their ways. Isaiah places it with feet running to wrongdoing and foolish thoughts. Romans retains its shorter chain clause rather than reproducing every surrounding charge.

Both passages speak of not knowing the way of peace. Isaiah adds the absence of justice and twisted paths, and uses its own present wording; Romans gives the shorter past-worded clause. Those additional accusations and formulations are not silently merged.

The no-fear-of-God-before-the-eyes statement corresponds to the psalm’s description of the lawless person. The psalm has his eyes, while Romans has their eyes within its collective chain. The singular lawless-person setting and his/their pronoun difference remain distinct.

Romans3 makes the whole world answerable to God as mouths are stopped. The later admonition says all the addressed community will stand before God’s judgment seat and each give account. The accountability corresponds, with world-versus-community scope and different immediate arguments retained.

Both passages deny justification by works of law, explicitly extending the denial to no flesh. Galatians also states faith in Jesus Christ; Romans adds that law brings knowledge of sin. Neither passage’s additional explanation is silently substituted for the other.

Romans says God’s revealed righteousness is witnessed by law and prophets even while describing it as apart from law. Jesus names the Law of Moses, Prophets and Psalms as writings about Him that must be fulfilled. The Scripture-witness connection does not make Luke repeat Paul’s apart-from-law formula or remove either role given to law here.

Romans connects righteousness with faith in Jesus Christ for all believers and no distinction. Galatians connects sonship with faith in Christ Jesus and says Jew and Greek and its additional categories are one in Him. The inclusion theme corresponds without treating righteousness and sonship as identical words or adding every Galatian category to this verse.

Romans concludes that all sinned and fall short of God’s glory. Solomon’s prayer introduces possible sin and captivity with the acknowledgment that no person will not sin. The human sin claim corresponds, while the glory language and the prayer’s possible captivity scenario are not transferred between statements.

Romans describes free justification by grace through redemption in Christ Jesus. Ephesians likewise speaks of redemption through His blood and forgiveness according to rich grace. The grace-and-redemption connection preserves justification versus forgiveness wording rather than making every clause a verbatim restatement.

Romans describes God setting Christ forth as propitiation in His blood through faith and discusses passing over earlier sins. The letter explicitly names Jesus Christ as advocate and propitiation for sins. The shared propitiation language does not make that target repeat every blood, faith or earlier-sins clause.

Romans joins God’s righteousness with justifying the one having faith in Jesus. The letter calls Him faithful and just to forgive and cleanse confessed sins. The divine justice and saving-action connection preserves the distinct faith/confession conditions and justification/forgiveness words instead of replacing one formulation with the other.

Romans excludes boasting through a law of faith rather than works. Ephesians describes salvation by grace through faith as God’s gift, not from works so that no one boasts. The exclusion corresponds, without making Ephesians repeat the law-of-faith expression.

Romans reckons a person justified by faith apart from works of law; James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. The comparison preserves works of law versus works and their different argument settings. It does not insert alone into Romans or supply an unreported explanation making the two statements verbatim equivalents.

Paul affirms that God is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews. Peter’s speech rejects divine partiality and accepts those fearing God and practicing righteousness in every nation. The national inclusion corresponds, while Peter’s stated response language and Paul’s faith-justification argument are not collapsed into one quotation.

Paul’s one-God premise accompanies justification of circumcised from faith and uncircumcised through faith. Deuteronomy’s address to Israel declares the Lord our God one. The monotheistic statement connects, but the faith clauses and their different prepositions are Paul’s formulation, not an added Deuteronomic line.

Paul rejects nullifying law through faith and speaks of establishing it. Jesus rejects coming to abolish Law or Prophets and speaks of fulfillment. The rejection of abolition connects, while establishing and fulfilling remain different words and neither passage is turned into an unquoted rule resolving every later law question.

The opening asks what Abraham has found; the ensuing argument explicitly turns to Scripture’s faith-and-righteousness statement about him. This identifies the proof text to which the question leads, not an independent account of his ancestry or every step of the works-and-boasting discussion.

Romans argues conditionally that works-based justification would give Abraham a boast, but not before God. James affirms justification in the Isaac-offering episode and describes faith working with works and brought to completion. The different arguments and use of the same righteousness Scripture remain visible, without adding an unstated before-humans versus before-God scheme.

The belief-in-God and reckoned-as-righteousness statement closely matches Genesis. Genesis here names Abram, whereas Romans uses Abraham. The later name form and the surrounding promise argument are retained without rewriting the earlier narrative’s actual name.

The wage illustration distinguishes what is owed to a worker from grace. The later remnant discussion likewise contrasts grace with works so that grace remains grace. The logical contrast connects distinct topics; the remnant statement is not another employment illustration or a claim that every wage is salvation.

Here the One justifies the ungodly and reckons the believer’s faith as righteousness. The later explanation describes Christ dying for the ungodly while they were weak. The undeserving recipients and saving provision connect, while death and faith-reckoning are distinct formulations rather than one repeated sentence.

Paul introduces David’s blessedness statement about reckoning righteousness apart from works. The saved psalm names David and pronounces forgiveness, covered sins and non-reckoning of sin. Paul’s righteousness-apart-from-works framing interprets those lines rather than pretending the psalm states every part of that introduction verbatim.

Both texts call blessed those whose lawless deeds are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Romans gives its own tense formulation within the argument. The psalm’s David-and-understanding heading remains original context and is not appended to the Pauline quotation.

The blessed man whose sin the Lord will certainly not reckon corresponds closely to this psalm line. The psalm additionally describes no deceit in his mouth; Romans does not include that additional clause in this quotation.

The circumcision question is supported by repeating that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness. Genesis narrates Abram believing God and the reckoning. The circumcised-versus-uncircumcised question is Paul’s application, not a question stated in that earlier verse.

Paul asks when righteousness was reckoned and answers before circumcision. Genesis15 supplies the earlier belief-and-reckoning event. That selected verse does not itself say uncircumcised; the later covenant-sign instructions provide the other part of Paul’s narrative-order argument.

The circumcision instructions and sign description occur later in Genesis than the belief-and-reckoning notice in15:6. This supplies the second event used by Paul’s before-circumcision argument, without manufacturing an exact elapsed interval or claiming these instructions repeat the earlier reckoning.

Genesis calls circumcision a sign of the covenant. Paul calls the received sign a seal of the righteousness of Abraham’s earlier faith and draws a fatherhood conclusion. The shared sign connects, while the seal, faith chronology and father-of-believers interpretation are not inserted into Genesis’s actual wording.

Romans describes circumcised people walking in Abraham’s prior faith rather than relying only on circumcision. Galatians calls people of faith Abraham’s sons and blesses them with believing Abraham. The faith-family relation corresponds, while the circumcision qualification and footstep image remain specific to Romans.

Both discussions connect Abraham, his seed, promise and inheritance while denying law as its basis. Galatians specifies Christ as seed and the later law’s430-year interval; Romans uses heir-of-the-world and righteousness-of-faith wording. Those different arguments and details are not transferred between passages.

Romans argues that making law the basis of heirship empties faith and nullifies promise. Galatians likewise says inheritance from law would no longer be from promise, whereas God granted it to Abraham through promise. The related contrast retains each argument’s actual faith and gift wording.

The law-wrath and no-law/no-transgression statement is followed later by sin existing before law but not being charged when no law exists. The relation to law connects, while sin, transgression and charging are not silently made identical or expanded into a claim that no wrongdoing exists apart from law.

Romans grounds the secure promise for all the seed in faith and grace, including both groups it names. Galatians describes those belonging to Christ as Abraham’s seed and heirs according to promise. The inclusive heirship connects without replacing Romans’s law-and-faith distinctions with an unquoted formulation.

The father-of-many-nations statement quotes the promise accompanying Abram’s change of name to Abraham. Romans adds its description of the God he trusted as giving life and calling what is not. Those added divine-ability clauses are not claimed to occur in this Genesis verse.

The so-shall-your-seed-be words recall the Lord taking Abram outside to consider the stars. Paul places the promise in an against-hope belief argument and many-nations conclusion. Genesis’s star image supplies the quoted setting without making every Pauline explanatory phrase part of the original speech.

Romans has Abraham consider his deadened body at about100 and Sarah’s womb without weakening in faith. Genesis records his hundred-year and Sarah’s ninety-year questions together with laughter. The shared age-and-parenthood setting retains the different response descriptions, without changing considered to did-not-consider or explaining the laughter’s unreported motive.

Romans describes Abraham strengthened in faith and giving glory to God over the promise. Hebrews describes Sarah beyond childbearing age receiving conception power because she considered the Promiser faithful. The family promise and faith correspond, while Sarah and Abraham and their particular response descriptions remain distinct.

Romans describes assurance that God can do what He promised. Hebrews has Abraham reason that God can even raise the dead in the Isaac-offering episode and calls the return figurative. The trust in divine ability corresponds across different episodes, without claiming that Isaac actually died or was bodily resurrected.

The therefore-reckoned-as-righteousness conclusion resumes the earlier cited belief-and-reckoning statement in Genesis. The narrative’s Abram name and original context are retained, while Paul draws his own conclusion from the preceding faith discussion.

Paul says the reckoning statement was not written for Abraham alone. The later general statement says earlier writings were for the readers’ instruction, perseverance, encouragement and hope. The application to later readers connects, without claiming every ancient text is the same sentence or was unrelated to its original recipient.

Romans applies the reckoning to believers in the One who raised Jesus our Lord. The letter similarly describes believers in God through Christ, God raising Him and giving Him glory. The God-directed faith and resurrection connect; the letter does not repeat the reckoned-righteousness wording.

Romans joins Jesus’ being handed over for trespasses and raised for justification. The Corinthian gospel summary likewise has Christ die for sins, be buried and be raised. Its third-day and according-to-Scripture details and Romans’s explicit justification purpose remain their separate formulations.

Romans describes justified-from-faith people having peace with God through Jesus Christ. Ephesians calls Christ our peace and describes reconciling both in one body to God through the cross. The peace relation corresponds, while the two-groups-and-barrier image and justification wording remain distinct.

Romans speaks of access through Christ by faith into grace, with standing and hope of glory. Ephesians likewise describes access through Him, but explicitly in one Spirit to the Father for both groups. The access connection preserves those different stated means, recipients and accompanying hope language.

Romans boasts in afflictions because they produce perseverance. James urges joy amid trials because testing faith produces endurance. The productive-trial relation corresponds, while boasting and counting joy and the affliction/testing formulations are not rewritten into one sentence.

Romans carries perseverance forward to proven character and hope. James gives testing-of-faith followed by endurance whose complete work leads to completeness. The endurance-and-formation connection retains the different order and final qualities, rather than claiming an identical character-and-hope sequence.

Romans names God’s love as what is poured into our hearts through the given Holy Spirit. Galatians says God sent His Son’s Spirit into our hearts, following its you-are-sons statement. The inward divine gift connects, while love being poured and the Spirit being sent remain distinct subjects and actions.

Romans has Christ die for the ungodly while they are weak, at the appointed time. The letter likewise has Christ suffer once for sins, righteous for unrighteous, being put to death to bring people to God. The recipients and death-for-sins connection correspond without importing every spirit/flesh or timing clause between them.

Romans reflects on the rarity of someone dying for a righteous or good person. Jesus’ saying names laying down life for friends as the greatest love. The self-giving comparison retains the different righteous/good versus friends categories and does not invent a named historical example behind the general statements.

Romans locates God’s demonstration of love in Christ dying for people still sinners. The letter locates manifested love in God sending His Son for life and as propitiation, prior to their loving God. The divine initiative connects, while the particular death, sending and propitiation formulations remain distinct.

Romans looks from justification in Christ’s blood to being saved through Him from wrath. The Thessalonian expectation likewise names Jesus as rescuing from coming wrath after His resurrection. The rescue corresponds, while the blood-justification premise and awaiting-from-heaven setting are not exchanged.

Both passages describe former enemies reconciled through death. Colossians names alienation in mind and evil works and presentation as holy; Romans argues from reconciliation through the Son’s death to salvation in His life. Those grounds and outcomes remain their actual formulations, with the following Colossian faith condition retained as context.

Romans boasts in God through Christ, through whom reconciliation has been received. The Corinthian account likewise attributes reconciliation to God through Christ and adds its ministry and message. The shared saving relation does not assign the identical ministry commission to every Roman recipient or erase the difference in the passages’ stated scope.

Romans’s one-person sin-and-death argument, naming Adam in the following discussion, connects with God addressing Adam for eating the forbidden tree and announcing return to earth. Genesis supplies that transgression-and-mortality setting; it does not itself state every universal causal clause in Paul’s because-all-sinned formulation or omit the woman’s part in the preceding story.

Romans5 says sin existed before law but is not charged when no law exists. Romans4 says law brings wrath and where no law exists there is no transgression. The related law-and-accountability claims retain their distinct sin/transgression/charging language rather than asserting no wrongdoing ever exists apart from law.

Romans calls Adam a type of the coming One while discussing death through the Adam-to-Moses period. Corinthians likewise contrasts the first human Adam with the last Adam, living soul versus life-giving spirit. The Adam-counterpart structure corresponds, while Moses, the temporal interval and soul/spirit language remain particular to their passages.

Romans contrasts the trespass’s many deaths with the greater gift in the grace of Jesus Christ. Corinthians contrasts death through a human being with resurrection through a human being and names Adam and Christ. The opposed outcomes correspond, while many versus all and grace-gift versus made-alive wording are not silently normalized.

Romans5 contrasts condemnation arising from one trespass with justification through the gift despite many trespasses. The later statement announces no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. The reversal of condemnation connects, without adding the earlier trespass counts or justification vocabulary to the later short statement.

Romans connects reception of abundant grace and righteousness with reigning in life through Jesus Christ. The saying connects dying with Him to living and enduring to reigning with Him. The life-and-reign language corresponds, with the distinct grace-reception and conditional-endurance formulations preserved.

Romans has all people in its condemnation and justification-of-life clauses; Corinthians has in Adam all die and in Christ all will be made alive. The paired Adam/Christ outcomes connect, but justification versus being made alive and the actual prepositional groupings are not rewritten or used to supply an unquoted decision about the extent of either all.

Romans opposes the one person’s disobedience and the One’s obedience through which the many will be made righteous. Philippians describes Christ Jesus becoming obedient to death on a cross. The obedience connects, while the explicit cross and many-made-righteous clauses belong to different passages.

Romans says law came alongside so the trespass might increase; Galatians says law was added because of transgressions until the seed came. The law-addition relation connects without changing so-that into because-of or moving the seed, angels and mediator details into Romans’s different grace-abounding statement.

Romans describes grace reigning through righteousness for eternal life through Jesus Christ. Titus likewise joins justification by grace with becoming heirs according to the hope of eternal life. The grace-and-life relation corresponds, while reigning and heirship are distinct images and their precise righteousness/justification wording is retained.

The question whether remaining in sin could increase grace recalls the rejected proposal to do evil for good to come. The earlier passage marks that proposal as slander with just condemnation. The connection identifies an argument being refused, not permission to increase sin or a claim Paul previously taught it.

Romans asks how those who died to sin can continue living in it. Colossians likewise says its hearers died and their life is hidden with Christ in God. The death-and-new-life contrast corresponds, but Romans’s explicit to-sin phrase is not inserted into the shorter Colossian claim or treated as a report of their physical deaths.

Both passages describe baptism into Christ. Romans explicates baptism into His death; Galatians describes putting on Christ. The shared baptismal relation preserves those different death and clothing images rather than making either statement repeat the other’s exact explanation.

Both passages join burial with Christ to baptism and raising. Romans names the Father’s glory and walking in newness of life; Colossians names being raised together through faith in God’s working. The corresponding pattern retains the distinct stated means and outcomes without adding one passage’s wording to the other.

Romans conditionally joins likeness of Christ’s death with future union in His resurrection. Colossians describes burial in baptism and already being raised together through faith in God’s working. The death-and-raising association connects, with the future and completed formulations left intact rather than forced into an identical timetable.

Romans’s old self is crucified with Christ so the body of sin may become powerless and enslavement cease. Galatians likewise says I have been crucified with Christ, then describes Christ living in the speaker. The shared crucifixion image retains the different body, slavery and indwelling explanations; the crucifixion clause actually belongs to the saved Galatians2:19 unit.

Romans says the one who died has been justified from sin within its death-with-Christ argument. Acts likewise speaks of justification in Him for believers from what Moses’ law could not justify. The justification-from language connects, while the conditions and formulations differ; justified is not silently replaced with freed or expanded into automatic salvation by any physical death.

Romans says that if we died with Christ we believe we will live with Him. The trustworthy saying likewise connects if-we-died-with-Him with future living with Him. The closely corresponding conditional retains Romans’s explicit believe clause and Christ name rather than claiming every word is identical.

Romans names the risen Christ as no longer dying and no longer under death’s rule. The Acts proclamation likewise says God raised Him from the dead never again to return to decay. The enduring risen-life claim corresponds, while death’s rule and the David-blessing citation remain their distinct explanatory language.

Romans describes Christ’s death to sin once for all and His life to God. Hebrews describes Christ offered once to bear many people’s sins and a second appearance for salvation. The once-and-sin relation connects, without making to-sin and bearing-sins identical phrases or inserting every later-appearance detail into Romans.

Romans urges the hearers to reckon themselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ. Colossians likewise names their death and life with Christ, with a future appearing in glory. The life-with-Christ correspondence retains reckon, hidden life and future revelation as different formulations.

Romans forbids sin’s rule in the mortal body and obedience to its desires. The letter urges abstention from fleshly desires that war against the soul. The shared resistance to desires preserves the different body-reign and soul-warfare images and the letter’s sojourner address.

Romans urges presenting bodily parts to God as weapons of righteousness rather than to sin as unrighteous weapons. Ephesians similarly uses a breastplate of righteousness with truth in its armor exhortation. The ethical military imagery connects, while body parts and worn armor are not treated as the same object or a verbatim command.

Romans says sin will not rule because the hearers are under grace rather than law. Galatians says those led by the Spirit are not under law. The shared not-under-law statement retains the distinct grace and Spirit-leading formulations rather than silently replacing either condition or calling law itself sin.

This question rejects sinning because the hearers are under grace rather than law. The earlier question rejects remaining in sin so grace increases. The differently framed temptations receive the same refusal; the comparison does not turn either rhetorical question into Paul’s recommended conduct.

Romans’s obedience illustration names slavery to sin leading to death, alongside obedience leading to righteousness. Jesus likewise calls everyone committing sin a slave of sin. The sin-slavery relation corresponds, while the death/righteousness alternatives are not added to John’s shorter statement.

Romans gives thanks for heart-obedience to the teaching pattern to which the hearers were handed over. The letter joins obedience to truth with purified souls and sincere love from a pure heart. The inward obedient response connects, while the direction of handing over and the particular teaching/cleansing formulations are not reversed or made identical.

Romans describes freedom from sin together with enslavement to righteousness. Jesus’ sin-slavery discussion likewise promises real freedom when the Son sets people free. The release corresponds, while the Son-and-house versus righteousness-service images remain distinct and do not become another account of literal manumission.

Romans6 urges presenting body parts to righteous service leading to sanctification. The later appeal likewise urges presenting bodies to God as a holy, pleasing living sacrifice. The embodied dedication corresponds, with slave-service and sacrifice retained as distinct images and no transfer of every earlier impurity or weakness clause.

The past state is slavery to sin and freedom from righteousness; the preceding statement reverses the terms to freedom from sin and enslavement to righteousness. The deliberate master-and-freedom contrast belongs to one argument, not independent testimony to a physical change of legal owner.

Romans6 asks about the shameful former fruit whose end is death. The later discussion likewise describes sinful passions working in bodily parts to bear fruit for death. The fruit-and-death relation corresponds without deciding an unreported biographical stage or replacing the later law-related explanation.

Romans describes fruit leading to sanctification and finally eternal life after freedom from sin and service to God. Galatians likewise contrasts fleshly corruption with reaping eternal life from the Spirit. The life-producing outcome connects, while fruit, sanctification, sowing and reaping remain different terms and images.

Romans calls death the wages of sin. James likewise gives a process in which desire conceives sin and fully grown sin gives birth to death. The death outcome connects, while payment and birth are different images and James’s desire sequence is not inserted into the shorter wage statement.

Romans contrasts sin’s wages with God’s gift of eternal life in Christ Jesus. The letter explicitly says God gave eternal life and that the life is in His Son, with having the Son linked to life. The divine gift and Christ/Son relation correspond without making John repeat the wage metaphor.

The premise that law rules a person during life is applied later as release from law after dying to what held the hearers. This traces the letter’s own death-and-release reasoning, not an independent general legal code or a claim that the law itself is the one who died.

Both passages describe a wife bound while her husband lives and free upon his death or falling asleep. Romans uses the illustration for the following law argument; Corinthians adds freedom to marry whom she wants only in the Lord. The contexts and additional qualification are not merged into an unquoted rule.

Romans explicitly calls belonging to another man adultery while the husband lives and denies that label after his death. Corinthians likewise distinguishes being bound during his life from freedom when he falls asleep. The binding/free principle corresponds, while Romans’s adultery label and Corinthians’s only-in-the-Lord condition remain their separate wording.

Romans describes the hearers put to death to law through Christ’s body, belonging to the risen One and bearing fruit to God. Galatians likewise says through law I died to law, was crucified with Christ and now live with Christ in me. The law-death and Christ-life connection retains the differing voices and marriage/fruit versus indwelling formulations.

Romans describes sinful passions working in bodily parts to bear fruit for death, with its explicit through-law relation. James likewise joins personal desire, conceived sin and death. The harmful progression corresponds, while the law clause and agricultural versus birth images are not silently exchanged.

Romans describes release to serve in Spirit newness rather than letter oldness. Corinthians likewise describes new-covenant ministry not of letter but Spirit, with killing versus life-giving language. The contrast connects without making service and ministry identical clauses or expanding letter into an unquoted rejection of all written Scripture.

Romans cites the prohibition as You shall not desire; the supplied Exodus uses covet and lists the neighbor’s wife and property. The command corresponds while the different English rendering and the target’s full object list are retained, rather than replacing either text to force a word-for-word match.

Romans7 makes sin the agent taking opportunity through the command and producing desire. The earlier discussion likewise links law’s arrival with trespass increasing. The related command/law setting preserves the different agency and purpose language, rather than declaring that law itself is sin or erasing the grace-abounding sequel.

The speaker describes being alive apart from law and sin coming to life when the command arrives. The preceding statement says sin is dead apart from law. The live/dead and command contrast connects directly without assigning the first-person voice a childhood age, conversion date or an unstated historical identity.

The command meant for life proves death to the speaker in Romans’s sin-through-command argument. Leviticus links doing God’s ordinances and judgments with living by them. The declared life relation and experienced death are compared without replacing sin as the Romans explanation’s agent or claiming Leviticus narrates this personal outcome.

Romans personifies sin deceiving the speaker through the command and killing him. Genesis has the woman report the serpent deceived her and she ate, within the forbidden-tree story. The deception-and-command setting connects without identifying the Romans I as that woman, sin as the serpent, or this selected Genesis verse as a report of her death.

Romans calls law holy and the command holy, righteous and good. The psalm likewise praises the Lord’s law, ordinances, command and judgments as blameless, upright, enlightening and true. The positive appraisal corresponds, preserving the distinct adjectives and not turning it into a quotation or praise of every human rule.

The question rejects making the good itself the cause of death and instead names sin working death through the good. This elaborates the earlier statement that sin used the command to deceive and kill. The agent/instrument relation is internal argument, not a second historical event or a rewriting of law as evil.

The first-person speaker is of flesh and sold under sin while describing law as spiritual. The earlier obedience illustration likewise names slavery to sin. The bondage metaphor connects, but its different voices and settings are retained rather than assigning the Romans I a fixed before-or-after conversion stage.

Romans’s speaker does what he hates rather than what he wants. Galatians likewise describes opposing flesh and Spirit so the hearers do not do the things they want. The will/action conflict corresponds, while Galatians’s named Spirit opposition is not automatically substituted for every law or mind term in Romans.

The unwilling action in Romans leads the speaker to agree that law is good. The letter likewise states law is good, with its explicit condition of lawful use. The appraisal connects, while neither the personal conflict nor the lawful-use qualification is silently made part of the other statement.

Romans says it is no longer I doing the action but sin dwelling in me; Galatians says I no longer live but Christ lives in me. The first-person indwelling formulas form a precise contrast with different actions and agents. The link does not identify sin with Christ or make both statements a single unqualified biographical stage.

The qualified no-good-in-my-flesh statement distinguishes willing good from accomplishing it. The earlier statement likewise contrasts what the speaker wants with what he actually does and hates. The recurring will/action problem preserves the in-my-flesh qualification rather than turning it into an unqualified assertion about every aspect of the person.

The failure to do wanted good and practice of unwanted evil restates the earlier doing-what-is-hated versus wanted contrast. These are repeated descriptions inside one argument, not independent occasions or evidence identifying the speaker’s precise life stage.

The if-I-do-what-I-do-not-want conclusion repeats no-longer-I-but-indwelling-sin from the earlier explanation. The conditional and repeated agency wording connect without adding a medical diagnosis, an unreported second personality or a separate historical episode.

Romans finds evil at hand when the speaker wants good. Galatians likewise locates wanted-action frustration in opposing flesh and Spirit desires. The opposition to willing corresponds, while their different named agents and Romans’s law-expression are not collapsed into one definition.

Romans’s speaker delights in God’s law in the inner self; the psalm’s speaker loves the Lord’s law and meditates on it all day.
